target_customer: Banks, fintech lenders and employers in Latin America, mainly Mexico, that need verified income and employment data for credit decisions
problem: Lenders in Latin America cannot easily verify the income of applicants, many of whom work informally or in the gig economy and have no credit history.

founders.name: José Carlos Aguilar
previous_startups: A gig economy lending company founded with the same co-founders (outcome not stated)
founders.background_notes: Uber background from the Contxto January 2022 article. Education not found.

founders.name: Pierre Delarroqua
previous_startups: A gig economy lending company founded with the same co-founders (outcome not stated)

founders.name: Antoine Nguyen Hong Duc
previous_startups: A gig economy lending company founded with the same co-founders (outcome not stated)
founders.background_notes: Listed as Antoine Nguyen in press. Education not found.

competitors.name: Argyle
competitors.what: US payroll and employment data API for income and employment verification
competitors.funding_then: About 22 million dollars total by late 2020 (2.6 million seed plus a 20 million Series A in late 2020), per a March 2022 article, a few months after the batch

competitors.name: Truework
competitors.what: US income and employment verification, mainly mortgage and tenant screening

technical_complexity.rationale: The team built integrations with gig and payroll platforms (Uber, DiDi, Rappi) and employer payroll systems, which means many brittle connections but no research-grade problem.

defensibility.rationale: Each payroll integration takes time to build and maintain, and lenders integrate the API into credit flows. By 2022 it covered 40 employers across six countries.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Experian did not copy it; it invested in the company in 2024 and led the May 2026 round per press.

market_need_then: The founders ran a gig economy lending company and found they could not validate earnings, so they built integrations that proved more valuable than the lending business. Many applicants in Latin America lack credit history.

identity.voice_and_tone: Professional, direct, B2B Spanish-language fintech tone with short declarative headlines and concrete metrics.

branding.brand_signature: Positioning as the income bureau for Latin America (The Work Number for LatAm)

rebrands.why: The YC directory and company website use Buró de Ingresos while press up to May 2026 uses Palenca. No source states the rebrand date or reason.

brand_strength.rationale: Little evidence of brand pull beyond B2B relationships. The descriptive new name echoes credit bureaus.

pivots.why: Founders found their data integrations more valuable than the lending business, per the August 2021 company blog post.

outcome_analysis: The company grew out of a failed or abandoned gig lending business whose founders knew the income verification pain first hand. It raised a 2.6 million dollar seed in January 2022, signed lenders such as Tarjeta Falabella Soriana, and in May 2026 raised 4 million dollars led by Experian while reporting about 5 million verifications in 2025. It is still active and no exit has occurred.
notes: The YC directory entry Buró de Ingresos matches the company called Palenca in press (Seedtable lists the Palenca seed under the Buró de Ingresos profile, the YC page links a Palenca news item, and the Palenca blog announces S21). The rebrand date is not sourced. Aggregators mention a 1 million dollar extension in April 2024 led by Experian, seen only in one aggregator so left unverified. The competitor list comes from an undated aggregator profile. YC page lists Founded 2026, which conflicts with the 2021 blog post.
